La mission silencieuse des Sœurs de Sain: The Silent Mission of the Sisters of Saint Ann
« Parfois, la meilleure chose à faire es: “Sometimes the best thing to do is to sit in silence and listen, since it’s indefensible”
Les communautés autochtones sont en deui: Indigenous communities across Canada are in mourning. On May 27, the unmarked remains of 215 Indigenous children were found at the site of the Kamloops residential school in British Columbia. The largest Indigenous residential school in Canada was overseen by the Sisters of Saint Ann, a congregation founded in Quebec in 1848. The Quebec nuns were employed and paid to force the assimilation of Indigenous children torn from their families, at no fewer than three other residential schools in British Columbia. At their motherhouse, the Sisters of Saint Ann’s legacy tied to the residential schools is kept low-key. Since the gruesome discovery, the nuns have held back. No Mass, no word, no comment, no apology. La Converse got them to break their silence. On Friday afternoon, after several days of insisting, we meet the superior of the Sisters of Saint Ann congregation, Sister Rita Larivée. She leads us through the small building that houses her office and gives us a guided tour of the heart of the Quebec congregation. “We are very invested in education and health,” she says, showing us artifacts from the sisters’ missions in Haiti, Chile, Cameroon, Japan, Alaska, Quebec and, finally, British Columbia. “That’s why you’re here,” she says, pointing to a glass case holding photos, pamphlets and a map showing the sisters’ journey from Montréal to Victoria. “Imagine sister Marie Jean Berchmans hurrying this way everyday and glancing across to her destination, the Songhees Indian School, where she taught from 1895-1911,” reads a pamphlet titled Following in Their Footsteps, displayed behind glass in the congregation’s small office, which we were able to consult. It is the only reference to the Sisters of Saint Ann’s involvement in the residential schools that we will find at the motherhouse.
La seule mention des pensionnats autocht: The only mention of Indigenous residential schools in the pamphlet “Following in Their Footsteps,” written by the congregation.
Sur le <l1>site internet</l1> des Sœurs,:
On the Sisters’ <l1>website</l1>, not a word about it. The Christian intuition of the convent’s founder is presented as “a legacy to share with Christians who feel called to make life grow.” “Mother Marie-Anne (Esther Blondin), founder of the congregation, is the evangelical figure who inspires them,” it says. Sister Larivée explains this by saying the congregation doesn’t have the technological resources to make changes to its website, since the nuns’ average age is 85. Her counterpart in British Columbia, Sister Marie Zarowny, says she has given presentations on the subject in Quebec schools. “We never denied our involvement in the residential schools, we participated fully in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. If people don’t know we were there, I don’t know why. We’re certainly not trying to hide anything.”

In recent days, numerous testimonies from Kamloops survivors have described the sexual and psychological abuse they suffered at the residential school. <l2>They were washed with disinfectant and told they would go to hell if they spoke their language, or references were made to the cemetery to discipline them.</l2> Asked about this, Sister Larivée first dwells on the nuns’ good intentions. “Yes, they were there, but at least they were there to take care of the children, because who else would have been there if it weren’t for them?” she asks, adding that they were “women of their time.” She attributes her congregation’s silence since the discovery at Kamloops to human failing. “To be honest, I have to say we were overwhelmed, because we were so involved; we didn’t know how to react. You can’t simply console yourself by saying, ‘I didn’t know.’ And you realize you were complicit.” Words fail her. “Sometimes the best thing to do is to sit in silence and listen, since it’s indefensible,” says the superior.
<strong>‍</strong>\n\nMais retournons en: ‍ But let’s go back to British Columbia, where 23 nuns from the congregation are still alive, and among them, some who worked at the Kamloops Indian Residential School (KIRS). The sisters refuse to give us their names or let us interview them, citing the protection of their privacy. “The people who were there know the names of the sisters who were there,” Sister Marie Zarowny, president of the Sisters of Saint Ann in British Columbia, tells us bluntly. On the phone, she says right away: “I want to clarify one thing: we never ran the Kamloops residential school. We were hired by another religious organization to administer the school, and our community was asked to provide teaching staff and support staff, to look after, among other things, the girls’ supervision and the food service.” Asked about the Sisters’ role, she responds by playing with words. “Whatever terminology is used, it probably doesn’t represent the meaning of what we were doing. [...] We were there to meet their needs, to take care of them, to entertain them; we were there to make sure they went to bed at the right time.” Within the congregation, we are referred to Sister Marie Zarowny’s work, in particular her efforts at dialogue with Indigenous nations. Despite this, she has not been in contact with survivors of the Kamloops residential school or with Indigenous leaders since the unmarked remains of 215 of the children her congregation educated were found. “I haven’t been in touch with survivors in the past week, and none of them has approached me. It is absolutely necessary that I have more information about these graves,” says Sister Zarowny. About the gruesome discovery, the president of the nuns in British Columbia is not ready to apologize. “We need to know why we would be apologizing and what really happened,” she says tersely. Her superior in Lachine, Sister Larivée, says that if she must apologize, the congregation will do so as a group, with the Canadian Religious Conference, that is, with the 240 Catholic congregations in the country. Why not an official apology on behalf of the Sisters of Saint Ann? “That’s just how we operate,” she retorts. The Sisters of Saint Ann looked after the children of KIRS from 1890 to 1970, but say they don’t know how many of them died. “Yes, students were dying, but even with our archives, we don’t know how many students died,” explains Sister Larivée. According to Sister Zarowny, when children died, they were buried at the residential school, in the cemetery, or sent to their families when possible. “Those who died were recorded. It’s not that children disappeared and we didn’t know what had happened to them; we were in mourning,” adds Sister Zarowny.
Les archives des sœurs pourraient éclair: The sisters’ archives could shed light on these questions, but they are hard to access. The nuns say they handed over all their archives on Indigenous residential schools to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation (NCTR) in 2012. “None of us has denied or withheld information about our involvement in the residential schools,” Sister Zarowny continues. “We participated fully in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.” When we ask to consult the archives, Sister Zarowny sends us to the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation. The Centre gives us a link that leads to a site stating that the archives are held at the Royal BC Museum. The archives are under lock and key and managed by an archivist from the Sisters of Saint Ann, who reviews them and notes inaccuracies. An agreement signed in 2011 and amended in 2018 was concluded between the Sisters of Saint Ann and the Royal BC Museum. Under this agreement, the archives remain under the nuns’ control until 2027. It is signed by Sister Marie Zarowny and the museum’s chief executive officer, Jach Lohman. Several members of British Columbia’s Indigenous communities are calling for the agreement to be broken and for an investigation into what led to its signing. This week, B.C. Minister of Arts and Culture Mélanie Mark also asked the Sisters of Saint Ann to hand over all their residential school archives to the affected Indigenous communities. Asked about this, the nuns say they were not informed of the requests from the minister and Indigenous communities. They dispute their statements. “Our archives have always been open to the public,” they say. According to Mary Ellen Turpel-Lafond, director of the Indian Residential School History and Dialogue Centre, even though the Sisters claim their archives are public, requests to consult them must be approved by one of the Sisters’ archivists, who has total control over the collection. “First Nations do not have clear or unimpeded access to the archives,” she sums up. She adds that when the Sisters of Saint Ann submitted documents to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, they did not sign a waiver, so those documents are not accessible. “It is time for the Sisters to acknowledge this fact and take concrete steps toward reconciliation by opening their files to First Nations who want a full account of these systems. This should not be put off until years from now,” she says. ‍
<strong>‍</strong>\n\nLa congrégation a: ‍ The congregation sent La Converse its own 25-page account of its legacy tied to the Kamloops residential school, drawn from its 109-page report The Sisters of Saint Ann in the Indian Residential Schools in British Columbia, Canada, 1868-1984: The Sisters’ Story. The document was written in 2015, after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearings. It praises the Sisters and “their tireless efforts” without mentioning the abuse the children endured. Anthropologist Marie-Pierre Bousquet has spent hours reading the archives of the religious congregations involved in the residential schools. “I’m stunned. Reading this, you’d think life at Kamloops was great. There is absolutely no critical perspective in light of the survivors’ testimonies; the children’s feelings are not part of these stories for them,” laments the director of the Indigenous studies program. She notes the tendency of religious congregations to embellish their experience, and this document is no exception. “These Indigenous children possess excellent qualities of mind and heart. They have good memories and learn easily. Their favourite subjects are drawing, arithmetic, history and geography, but they are eager to learn religion. The boys are diligent, the girls are skilful. All have a remarkable talent for music and singing,” it reads. “I get the impression this was written in 1935, not 2015,” says the researcher. “Complicit in a destructive system” At the Sisters of Saint Ann’s motherhouse, in the small park near the convent’s cemetery, a set of life-size statues shows the congregation’s founder playing with two children. Inside the building, on the walls of the fifth floor, hangs a necrology board listing all the sisters of the congregation who have died since 1850. Among them are some who worked in Indigenous residential schools. The nuns let us photograph them, but then ask us not to publish the photos. “Did they take part in a genocide?” we ask Sister Larivée. “They were unwittingly complicit in a destructive system that systematically aimed to destroy a culture,” she answers. “I wouldn’t go so far as to say our sisters took part in a cultural genocide,” she tells us. We then ask her whether, after the discovery of the mass graves at Kamloops, she, the superior of the Sisters of Saint Ann congregation, is prepared to acknowledge that Indigenous residential schools were at the root of a genocide. “These policies, which were promoted by the Canadian government, we can now look back and say it was a cultural genocide, I would be ready to go that far, yes. As for calling it a genocide outright, I would need more information.” ‍

The nuns often invoke the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) when asked about their responsibility. The commission was created while residential school survivors were bringing a $12-billion class action against Canada and the Vatican. The TRC had no subpoena power. Church officials and the government could therefore not be summoned to court. Several experts we spoke to question the type of justice it produced. Marie-Pierre Bousquet, director of the Indigenous studies program at UdeM, believes the TRC limited the damage and protected the religious orders.

But that could change. Lawyers from across the country have asked the International Criminal Court to <l1>investigate the Canadian government and the Vatican for crimes against humanity</l1> following the discovery of the hidden cemetery at Kamloops. The congregations involved could be legally charged and found responsible for crimes against humanity. Asked about this, Sister Rita Larivée answers: “We were only employees, we weren’t the administrators.” It is an argument heard in many war crimes trials: in Yugoslavia, in Rwanda and after the Holocaust. “Yes, that’s true,” she admits timidly. “Can we prosecute people who were following the law? We must find ways to move toward healing, I don’t think punitive law is the right road to take,” the nun justifies herself.

The Sisters’ motherhouse will close its doors in December. In Quebec, and elsewhere in Canada, religious vocations are increasingly rare. The nun estimates that in fifteen years or so, the Sisters of Saint Ann will be nothing more than a legacy. The average age, she repeats, is 85. Will the nuns be more transparent about their past in Indigenous residential schools? “It’s part of our legacy, but it’s not our whole legacy. It may not be perfect, but our intention is to do the best we can so that history doesn’t repeat itself. We are trying to build a better future, without denying part of our legacy.”

What do the sisters say to the survivors of Kamloops and to the survivors’ children? An hour and a quarter into the interview, Sister Larivée breathes out the three words many are asking to hear: “We’re sorry.” “We are sorry, we weep with you, we weep with your children and we will do everything to walk with you toward healing.” So, are you apologizing? we ask. “I think we have to apologize, I think we have to sincerely say ‘I’m sorry,’ and we are all sorry,” she concludes.

A few hours after our conversation, the Canadian Religious Conference expressed its sadness and compassion, without apologizing, in <l2>a statement Sister Rita sent us</l2>.

<strong>Pour aller plus loin...</strong>: Going further... The Sisters’ role in Indigenous residential schools
« Dans ces écoles, les religieuses sont: “In these schools, the nuns were placed directly under the authority of the male congregation in charge of the institution, very generally the Oblates of Mary Immaculate. To administer these residential schools and to specify the roles and duties of the male and female congregations present, contracts were drawn up between the two co-managing congregations. The nuns are designated in them as ‘collaborators.’ The contracts specify that they were to be responsible for instruction during class hours, but also for the children’s education in the evenings and on weekends, accompanying them during meals, care, chores and recreation. These contracts also underline the ‘auxiliary’ position reserved for the nuns in these establishments. They were responsible for the internal management of the residence: the children’s living quarters and the Fathers’ house. Through their constant presence, they were the ones in charge of transforming the children, from a very young age, with a view to their assimilation. They were the main actors in the transmission of the many kinds of knowledge, know-how and social skills that young Indigenous people were required to acquire under the policy then in place. Beyond their teaching activity, the nuns in residential schools became, in a way, substitute mothers. Several sisters interviewed indicated that they had to play the ‘role of parents’ for the children in their care,” writes Marion Robinaud, anthropologist and author of a study titled Les pensionnats indiens au Canada. Les religieuses et la transmission des savoirs pour l’assimilation des autochtones.
« Toujours avide de faire du bien parmi: “Always eager to do good among the young, even in foreign lands still uncivilized, the Sisters of Saint Ann opened a mission in Kamloops in 1880,” we read in the book Les Sœurs de Sainte-Anne, by Marie-Jean de Patmos.

And that would not be their last stop,” wrote Lionel Groulx in his book Le Canada français missionnaire.
